title: [Performance]: Waiting requests re-walk their whole prefix-cache hit on every scheduling step
body:
### Proposal to improve performance

When a waiting request cannot be admitted, which is typical under KV-cache pressure, it stays at the head of the waiting queue and `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` → `find_longest_cache_hit` runs again on every step. The walk probes the block-hash table once per hit block, so a request with a long cached prefix pays for the whole walk again on every retry, on the scheduler thread.

I have a local implementation of a narrow fix and would like to know whether this is worth a PR before sending one, because it touches `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py` (+126/−5, plus tests) and I could not show an end-to-end gain.

**Idea.** Keep each waiting request's previous hit together with the primary `block_hash` each hit block carried. On the next lookup, keep the remembered blocks up to the first one whose hash changed, and resume the normal walk from there. A block keeps its primary hash exactly as long as it stays cached with unchanged contents, because eviction, hash moves and `reset_prefix_cache` all clear it, so the result equals a full walk. The memo is enabled only for a single full-attention group (`UnitaryKVCacheCoordinator`), with no EAGLE drop and DCP = PCP = 1; everything else keeps the current path. Under KV pressure the hit usually changes only at its tail, which is why per-block revalidation beats invalidating a cached result on any eviction.

**What I measured** (main `a2fb482732`, CPU only, scheduler driven directly with no model forward; workload: 8192-token shared prefix + 256 suffix, 384 output tokens, 2400 × 16-token blocks, 64 running, 400 requests; 5 seeds).

| | main | with the memo |
|---|---|---|
| scheduling decisions, per step | — | byte-identical (sha256 of the decision trace, all seeds) |
| hash-table probes | 736,080 | 265,150 (−64%) |
| total lookup time | 313.3 ms | 159.4 ms |
| total `schedule()` time | 1223.8 ms | 1137.4 ms (~−7%, near the ±3% run-to-run noise) |

A single lookup with a still-valid 2048-block hit drops from 956.5 to 75.8 µs.

**What I could not show.** An end-to-end serving A/B (RTX 4090, Qwen3-1.7B, the same workload shape via `prefix_repetition`, 3 alternating rounds) showed no measurable difference: 1577.10 vs 1574.66 output tok/s, inside main's own spread of 1573–1597. At ~33 ms per decode step, ~0.2 ms saved per blocked lookup is too small to see. It might matter with larger prefixes, smaller step times, or many long-prefix requests blocked at once, but I have not measured such a setup.

**Questions for maintainers**

1. Is shaving scheduler CPU time in this scenario something you would take in `kv_cache_manager.py` at this size, or is the bar a demonstrated end-to-end gain?
2. If it is of interest, is there a workload or configuration where you have seen waiting-queue prefix lookups show up in profiles? I can benchmark against that instead.

Related but different: #58837 and #54625 change admission *order* based on cache hits, and #61570 speeds up block-pool and hashing hot paths. None of them avoids re-walking the same waiting request's hit.

AI assistance was used to investigate this and draft this issue. I reviewed the code and ran every measurement above myself.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

CPU measurements: WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04, 32 vCPU, Python 3.12.3, torch 2.13 (CPU). GPU A/B: RTX 4090 24 GB, driver 595.71.05, torch 2.13.0+cu130.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
